title: A Second Practice Story
teaser: Another practice story used to rehearse the one-tap release. It is never shown to readers.
story: As a young man in Beijing, Wang Yangming and a friend surnamed Qian decided to take the great twelfth-century philosopher Zhu Xi at his word. Zhu Xi taught that the road to becoming a sage began with 'investigating things': finding the pattern, or principle, in whatever you meet. So the two of them sat before the bamboo in front of a pavilion and tried to find its pattern. Qian worked at it day and night and fell ill on the third day. Wang carried on alone and fell ill on the seventh. They concluded that becoming a sage was beyond them.

Wang passed the highest civil service examination in 1499 and became an official. In 1506 he spoke up for two officials, Dai Xian and Bo Yanhui, who had been arrested on the orders of the powerful eunuch Liu Jin. For that he was stripped and given forty strokes in public, imprisoned for several months, and banished. In the spring of 1508 he reached Longchang, a courier station in the hills of Guizhou, in China's south-west, as its station master. He was often ill there. When his three attendants fell sick too, he cut firewood, cooked porridge and told them stories. He made himself a stone coffin and lay in it, asking what a sage would do in his place.

One night, aged 36, he had his answer. The principles he had hunted for in the bamboo were not out there in things. They were to be found by looking within his own mind. The following year an education official, Xi Shu, came to ask him about the rival schools of Confucian thought. Wang answered with the idea he is now best known for: the unity of knowledge and action.

Most of us assume that knowing comes first and doing follows, and that the gap between them is where we fail. Wang denied the gap. His student Xu Ai objected that everyone knows they should be filial to their parents, yet plenty aren't. Wang replied: 'No one has ever known but failed to act.' Someone who claims to know but doesn't act doesn't yet truly know. He pointed to a line in the Great Learning, a Confucian classic, about loving a lovely sight and hating a hateful odour. 'Seeing a lovely sight belongs to knowledge, while loving a lovely sight belongs to action.' You don't see the sight and then decide to love it: the two arrive together. A person with a blocked nose, Wang said, doesn't truly know a bad smell at all. Real moral knowledge, for him, works the same way.

Liu Jin was executed in 1510, and Wang's exile ended. He went on to serve as a governor and a general, captured a rebel prince, and died in 1529. His recorded last words were: '"This mind" is luminous and bright. What more is there to say?'
When we say we know we should sleep more or speak more kindly, and don't, Wang would say we know it only as a phrase, not the way we know the smell of something rotten.
takeaway: The unity of knowledge and action: Wang Yangming held that to truly know what is right is already to be moved to do it, so knowing but not doing means you don't yet really know.

recall.question: Castiglione's courtiers at Urbino prized a quality that makes difficult things look easy. What is it called, and what is its catch?
recall.answer: Sprezzatura. The ease has to be earned, and the moment the effort to look effortless shows, the spell breaks.

rabbitHole.title: Mind over bamboo
rabbitHole.intro: Wang's bamboo vigil is one of the most retold stories in Chinese philosophy. Follow it down, from a pavilion in Beijing to a burning warehouse district in Osaka.

levels.heading: Was the bamboo a fair test?
body: The popular version has Wang staring at bamboo, proving Zhu Xi's method hopeless, and founding a new school. The evidence is less tidy. Zhu Xi, following the earlier philosopher Cheng Yi, described extending knowledge as 'encountering things and exhaustively investigating their Pattern', building on what you already understand until, after long effort, it suddenly comes together. He did think the Pattern was present even in ordinary objects, but he said the best way to learn it was to study the classics, especially the Four Books.

So, as the philosopher Bryan Van Norden puts it, it is questionable whether sitting before bamboo is what Zhu Xi had in mind. The story is better read as Wang's account of how the method failed him than as a refutation of it. Even the date is uncertain. Ping Dong's biography places the episode when Wang was about 16 and living in Beijing; another Chinese account dates it to 1492, when he was 21.

levels.heading: What counts as knowing
body: Wang's word for the knowledge that can't be separated from action is zhen zhi, genuine knowledge. Ordinary 'knowing that' something is true doesn't count. He liked examples you can only learn first-hand: 'If you want to know bitterness, you have to eat a bitter melon yourself.' Behind this sits liangzhi, innate knowing, an idea he took from Mencius. Everyone has it, Wang taught; it can't be lost, only obscured by selfish desire.

Philosophers still argue about what genuine knowledge actually is. The philosopher Harvey Lederman sets out four ways of reading it: as a kind of perception, as practical know-how, as knowing what you ought to do, or as introspective knowledge of your own mind. He argues that the last fits Wang's texts best. Wang insists that genuine knowledge doesn't come before action, and the practical and normative readings struggle to explain that.

levels.heading: Across the sea
body: In Japan, Wang's philosophy became Yōmeigaku. Its leading followers included Nakae Tōju (1608–1648) and Kumazawa Banzan (1619–1691), and it inspired some leaders of the Meiji Restoration of 1868.

Its most dramatic follower was Ōshio Heihachirō, a former official in Osaka's city magistrate's office who ran a school of Wang Yangming learning. During the famine of the 1830s he accused the authorities of taking no measures to help the starving people of Osaka. In 1837 he rose against them. His followers distributed rice from warehouses, and placards declared, in Joshua Fogel's translation of Masuda Wataru, 'We are not rising out of a desire to seize the realm for ourselves.' The rising was crushed in a day, more than 3,000 houses burned, and Ōshio died weeks later in a fire as officials closed in.

furtherReading.title: Wang Yangming
furtherReading.author: Bryan Van Norden, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (2014, revised 2019)
furtherReading.note: A clear survey of Wang's philosophy and the objections to it.

lookingGlass.heading: Knowing better, doing worse
body: The obvious objection is the one Xu Ai raised, and it has never gone away. Van Norden sets out the problems. Wang's favourite examples, pain and hunger, show at most that you must have felt something once to know it, not that knowing it moves you now. People can know that someone is hungry, or that plagiarism is wrong, without being moved at all. And even a real pull needn't end in action: finding someone attractive doesn't mean pursuing them.

Other Confucians went further. The Ming scholar Luo Qinshun called the identification of mind and principle 'an infinitesimal mistake in the beginning leading to an infinite error at the end'. Later Qing scholars dismissed Song and Ming thinkers, Wang included, for 'empty words', and Dai Zhen faulted them for treating subjective opinions as infallible moral guidance.
lookingGlass.verdict: Where that leaves you: use Wang's idea as a test rather than a law, asking whether you know a thing the way you know a bad smell, without assuming that every lapse is ignorance.

quiz.question: What happened when Wang Yangming and his friend Qian tried to find the pattern in bamboo?
options: Both fell ill, and they decided becoming a sage was beyond them
Wang found the pattern on the seventh day and wrote it down
Zhu Xi praised them for following his method
They were punished for neglecting their official duties
quiz.explain: Qian fell ill on the third day and Wang on the seventh. Wang only found his answer years later in exile at Longchang, by looking within his own mind.

quiz.question: On Wang's unity of knowledge and action, what should we say about someone who claims to know they should care for their parents, but doesn't?
options: They don't yet truly know it
They know it perfectly but lack willpower
They know it, and acting on it is a separate skill to be learned
They know it but are excused by circumstances
quiz.explain: Answering Xu Ai, Wang said 'No one has ever known but failed to act.' Real knowing is like smelling a bad odour: the hating comes with the knowing.
